raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to solve a paradox created by durable metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): the need for transient radial support and antiproliferative drug delivery, but not for a permanent metallic cage. The theoretical advantages—restored vasomotion, adaptive remodeling, easier future bypass grafting, less late neoatherosclerosis, and improved non-invasive imaging—made the “leave nothing behind” concept compelling [1]. Early experience with the poly-L-l-lactide everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold showed feasibility in simple de novo lesions, with multimodality imaging suggesting late strut disappearance, luminal enlargement, and some recovery of vasoreactivity [2–4].

The subsequent randomized evidence was more sobering. In ABSORB III, Absorb was non-inferior to cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents at 1 year for target-lesion failure, but numerically increased device thrombosis was already apparent [5]. At 3 years, target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis were significantly higher with BVS, particularly in very small vessels [6]. Five-year ABSORB III follow-up suggested that the excess hazard was concentrated before complete scaffold resorption, with less divergence beyond 3 years [7]. ABSORB IV, designed after recognition of the importance of lesion selection and optimized implantation, still showed a modest but significant 5-year excess in target-lesion failure despite improved technique [8].

Other randomized trials confirmed the pattern. ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan met early angiographic or clinical non-inferiority criteria in selected lesions [9,10]. ABSORB II failed to show superiority for vasomotion and showed more late lumen loss and adverse events, with persistent concern at 4 years [11,12]. In the all-comers AIDA trial, target-vessel failure was similar, but scaffold thrombosis was substantially higher with BVS [13]. Patient-level meta-analyses consistently demonstrated acceptable 1-year efficacy but higher 2- and 3-year rates of target-lesion failure, myocardial infarction, and device thrombosis [14–16]. These data led to withdrawal or marked restriction of first-generation Absorb use in routine PCI.

Why did an elegant concept fail clinically? The principal factors were mechanical and procedural. Absorb had thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, lower acute radial strength than metallic DES, and radiolucency that complicated deployment. Scaffold underexpansion, malapposition, implantation in small vessels, discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy, and insufficient post-dilatation were linked to thrombosis [17,18]. This led to the “PSP” strategy—adequate predilatation, appropriate sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—often aided by intravascular imaging. Although PSP improved acute results, randomized data indicate that technique alone did not fully overcome first-generation device limitations [8,19].

Special populations have not rescued the technology. In STEMI, the theoretical benefit of late vessel restoration is attractive, and TROFI II showed comparable early optical healing in selected patients [20]. However, acute thrombotic lesions, vasoconstriction, and sizing uncertainty magnify scaffold risks. In higher restenosis-risk lesions, COMPARE-ABSORB achieved non-inferiority for 1-year target-lesion failure but showed higher device thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction, reinforcing the need for caution in complex anatomy [21].

The field has therefore shifted from proving the concept to redesigning the platform. Magnesium-based scaffolds, exemplified by DREAMS 2G/Magmaris, offer faster resorption, improved radiopacity, and potentially better early mechanical behavior. BIOSOLVE-II and BIOSOLVE-IV reported low scaffold thrombosis and acceptable clinical outcomes in selected lesions and registries [22–24]. Other polymeric platforms, including MeRes100, DESolve, and XINSORB, have pursued thinner struts, improved visibility, greater expansion latitude, and modified resorption kinetics, with encouraging early angiographic or clinical results [25–27]. However, most remain supported by single-arm studies, modest randomized trials, or geographically limited evidence.

Current PCI practice therefore favors contemporary metallic DES for almost all routine coronary lesions. BVS should be considered investigational or highly selective, ideally within trials, using careful lesion selection, intravascular imaging, and meticulous implantation. The lesson of Absorb is not that bioresorption is biologically futile, but that scaffolds must match or exceed metallic DES in acute deliverability, expansion, thrombosis resistance, and early safety before any late benefit can matter [28–30].
